cse-1995-a-47.approach: Judge each statement on its own, then pick the option listing exactly the true ones.

steps.title: Statements I and II
steps.body:
**I** — with a fixed table size, more keys means a higher load factor $\alpha = n/m$, so collisions increase: **true**.

**II** — recursion adds call/return overhead and stack space; recursive programs are not inherently efficient: **false**.

steps.title: Statements III and IV
steps.body:
**III** — quicksort on already-sorted input with a first/last-element pivot gives partitions of sizes $n-1$ and $0$: $T(n)=T(n-1)+O(n)=O(n^2)$: **true**.

**IV** — a linked list has no $O(1)$ access to the middle element, so each probe costs $O(n)$ traversal; binary search loses its advantage: **false**.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: True statements: I and III → option **D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: II is false — recursion carries call overhead.
II is false, even though III is true.
IV is false — finding the middle of a linked list takes linear time.
I and III are both true.

pitfalls: Thinking binary search is $O(\log n)$ on any sorted structure — it needs random access.
cse-1995-a-47.verification: Quicksort on 1,2,…,n with first-element pivot does $(n-1)+(n-2)+\dots+1 = n(n-1)/2$ comparisons, confirming III.

cse-1995-a-48.approach: We need a synchronizing sequence that ends in C from every start state: track the set of possible current states as each input is applied.

steps.title: Length-1 inputs
steps.body:
Start set $\{A,B,C,D\}$.

- input 1: $A\to D, B\to B, C\to B, D\to B$ → $\{B,D\}$
- input 0: $A\to B, B\to C, C\to D, D\to C$ → $\{B,C,D\}$

Neither is $\{C\}$, so no single input works.

steps.title: Try 10
steps.body: After 1: $\{B,D\}$. Apply 0: $B\to C$, $D\to C$ → $\{C\}$. Every start state ends in C.

steps.title: Check 01
steps.body: After 0: $\{B,C,D\}$. Apply 1: $B\to B, C\to B, D\to B$ → $\{B\}$, not C. So **10** is the shortest sequence.

optionAnalysis.reason: 01 always ends in B, not C.
1 takes every state to {B, D}; 0 then takes both to C.
101 ends in {B} (10 gives C, then 1 gives B), and it is longer anyway.
110: 1→{B,D}, 1→{B}, 0→{C} works but has length 3, not the shortest.

pitfalls: Reading the columns in the wrong order — the x = 1 column comes first in the table.
cse-1995-a-48.verification: Traced 10 from each start state separately: A→D→C, B→B→C, C→B→C, D→B→C.

cse-1995-a-49.approach: Union with $\Sigma^*$ gives $\Sigma^*$ itself; $0^n1^n$ is the textbook non-regular language.

steps.title: L ∪ R
steps.body: $R \subseteq \Sigma^* = L$, so $L\cup R = \Sigma^*$, which is regular (accepted by a 1-state DFA).

steps.title: The language R
steps.body: $R=\{0^n1^n : n>0\}$ needs unbounded counting. Pumping lemma: for $w=0^p1^p$, any split with $|xy|\le p$ puts $y$ inside the 0s, and $xy^2z = 0^{p+|y|}1^p \notin R$. So R is **not regular**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $L\cup R=\Sigma^*$ is regular, and R is not.
A union can be regular even when one part is not — here it is $\Sigma^*$.

pitfalls: Assuming the union of a regular and a non-regular language must be non-regular.
cse-1995-a-49.verification: Known result: a superset of a non-regular language can be regular, and $\Sigma^*$ is a superset of every language over $\Sigma$.

cse-1995-a-50.approach: WORD bits come from the block size; SET bits come from the number of sets, which is the cache size divided by (block size × associativity).

steps.title: WORD field
steps.body: 64 words per block → $\log_2 64 = 6$ bits.

steps.title: SET field
steps.body: Blocks in cache $= 4096/64 = 64$. Sets $= 64/4 = 16$ → $\log_2 16 = 4$ bits.

optionAnalysis.reason: 15 bits for SET would mean 32K sets — far more than the cache holds.
6 is the WORD field width (or the number of block bits); SET is 4.
7 and 2 match no part of the calculation.

pitfalls: Using the number of blocks (64 → 6 bits) instead of the number of sets.

cse-1995-a-51.approach: Convert to decimal, do each operation, then wrap the result to the width of the destination (8 bits for bytes, 16 bits for Z) and flag any value that does not fit.

steps.title: X := A + B
steps.body: $92 + 146 = 238 \le 255$ → fits in a byte. $238 = 14\cdot16+14$ → **X = EEH**, no error.

steps.title: W := A − B
steps.body: $92 - 146 = -54$, which cannot be stored in an unsigned byte → **underflow / range error**. The bits stored (two's-complement wrap) are $256-54 = 202 = 12\cdot16+10$ → **W = CAH**.

steps.title: Z := A * B
steps.body: $92 \times 146 = 13432 \le 65535$ → fits in two bytes. $13432 = 3\cdot4096 + 4\cdot256 + 7\cdot16 + 8$ → **Z = 3478H**, no error.

answer.value: X = EEH, Y = 36H, W = CAH (A − B is negative: underflow for an unsigned byte), Z = 3478H

pitfalls: Forgetting that W is unsigned: −54 is out of range, so only W raises an error condition.
Assuming A*B overflows — Z is a 2-byte integer, and 13432 fits.

cse-1995-a-52-a.approach: GET follows Pascal's rule $C(A,B)=C(A-1,B)+C(A-1,B-1)$ with $C(\cdot,0)=1$ and $C(A,B)=0$ for $A<B$, so GET(A, B) $=\binom{A}{B}$. Expanding the calls confirms it.
pitfalls: Missing the base case $A<B$, which returns 0 before B = 0 is reached.
cse-1995-a-52-a.verification: Pascal's identity with the same boundary values gives $\binom{A}{B}$; $\binom{3}{2}=3$ matches the trace.

cse-1995-a-52-b.approach: A transpose must swap each off-diagonal pair once. With J running over 1..N, every pair (I, J) and (J, I) is swapped twice, which puts it back where it started.

steps.title: What the code does
steps.body:
Take $N=2$: I runs 1..1 and J runs 1..2.

- $J=1$: swaps $A[1,1]$ with itself.
- $J=2$: swaps $A[1,2]$ and $A[2,1]$.

For $N\ge3$, a pair with $I<J\le N-1$ is swapped at $(I,J)$ and again at $(J,I)$, so it is restored. A pair in column N is swapped only once. The result is not the transpose.

steps.title: Correction
steps.body:
Only swap above the diagonal:

```pascal
for I := 1 to N-1 do
  for J := I+1 to N do
    begin
      TMP := A[I,J];
      A[I,J] := A[J,I];
      A[J,I] := TMP
    end
```
Each pair $(I,J)$ with $I<J$ is now swapped exactly once.

answer.value: The inner loop should be `for J := I+1 to N do`

pitfalls: Changing only the outer bound — the double swap comes from the inner loop starting at 1.
cse-1995-a-52-b.verification: For $N=3$ with the fix: the swaps are (1,2), (1,3), (2,3), which are the three off-diagonal pairs, each swapped once.

cse-1995-a-53-a.approach: Simulate both policies on the hole list. After Job 1 leaves, the holes are 0–200k (200k) and 850–1000k (150k); First Fit takes the lowest-address hole that fits, Best Fit takes the smallest hole that fits.

steps.title: Best Fit
steps.body:
- J4 (120k): smallest hole ≥ 120k is 150k → **850–970k**; holes 0–200k (200k), 970–1000k (30k).
- J5 (150k): only 200k fits → **0–150k**; holes 150–200k (50k), 970–1000k (30k).
- J6 (80k): holes 50k and 30k are too small → **cannot be allocated** (80k free in total, but split up).

| region | Best Fit |
|---|---|
| 0–150k | J5 |
| 150–200k | free (50k) |
| 200–550k | J2 |
| 550–850k | J3 |
| 850–970k | J4 |
| 970–1000k | free (30k) |

answer.value: First fit: J4 at 0-120k, J5 at 850-1000k, J6 at 120-200k (all fit). Best fit: J4 at 850-970k, J5 at 0-150k, J6 cannot be allocated (holes of 50k and 30k).

pitfalls: Letting Best Fit put J4 into the 200k hole — the 150k hole is the tighter fit.
cse-1995-a-53-a.verification: Memory accounting: First Fit uses 120+80+350+300+150 = 1000k exactly; Best Fit uses 920k with 80k free but split into 50k + 30k.

cse-1995-a-53-b.approach: Compare the outcomes from part (a): the better algorithm here is the one that places every job.

steps.title: Outcomes from part (a)
steps.body:
**First Fit** places J4, J5 and J6; memory ends 100% used.

**Best Fit** places J4 and J5 but J6 (80k) fails, although 80k is free in total — it is split into 50k + 30k holes.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: For this sequence **First Fit** performs better. Best Fit's tight placement of J4 into the 150k hole left the 200k hole for J5, which created two unusable fragments.

pitfalls: Assuming Best Fit is always better — it tends to leave tiny unusable holes.
cse-1995-a-53-b.verification: Re-checked the hole lists in part (a): First Fit ends with no free memory; Best Fit ends with holes of 50k and 30k and J6 waiting.

cse-1995-a-54.approach: In postorder the root comes last, so C is the root for every tree. For a fixed shape, the postorder sequence fixes the labels uniquely, so the count equals the number of binary-tree shapes with 3 nodes: the Catalan number $C_3 = 5$.

steps.title: Count the shapes
steps.body:
Number of binary trees with $n$ nodes $= \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$. For $n=3$: $\frac{1}{4}\binom{6}{3} = \frac{20}{4} = 5$.

Each shape gets exactly one labelling: fill its nodes in postorder with A, B, C.

steps.title: Tree 1: left chain
steps.body: C has left child B; B has left child A. Postorder: A, B, C.

steps.title: Tree 2: left, then right
steps.body: C has left child B; B has right child A. Postorder: A, B, C.

steps.title: Tree 3: balanced
steps.body: C has left child A and right child B. Postorder: A, B, C.

steps.title: Tree 4: right, then left
steps.body: C has right child B; B has left child A. Postorder: A, B, C.

steps.title: Tree 5: right chain
steps.body: C has right child B; B has right child A. Postorder: A, B, C.

pitfalls: Only counting trees with A and B as children of C (option 3) — the chains also give postorder A, B, C.
cse-1995-a-54.verification: Postorder of each drawn tree: chains visit the deepest node first, then its parent, then C; the balanced tree visits left A, right B, then C. All five give A, B, C, and the five shapes are distinct.

cse-1995-a-55-a.approach: Factorise into primes; a divisor picks each prime exponent independently, so the count is the product of (exponent + 1).
pitfalls: Forgetting the $+1$ for the zero exponent (which accounts for divisors such as 1 and 3).
cse-1995-a-55-a.verification: Divisors pair up as $d \cdot (600/d)$ with $\sqrt{600}\approx24.5$; the divisors ≤ 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20, 24 — 12 of them — so there are $2\times12=24$.

cse-1995-a-55-b.approach: Use the geometric inequality $\sin x < x < \tan x$ for $0<x<\pi/2$ (areas of a triangle, sector and triangle in the unit circle) and the squeeze theorem.

steps.title: Area inequality
steps.body:
In the unit circle with angle $x\in(0,\pi/2)$:

$$\underbrace{\tfrac12\sin x}_{\text{inner triangle}} < \underbrace{\tfrac12 x}_{\text{sector}} < \underbrace{\tfrac12\tan x}_{\text{outer triangle}}$$

so $\sin x < x < \tan x$.

steps.title: Rearrange
steps.body:
Divide by $\sin x>0$: $1 < \dfrac{x}{\sin x} < \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$, so

$$\cos x < \frac{\sin x}{x} < 1.$$

All three terms are even functions, so this also holds for $-\pi/2<x<0$.

steps.title: Squeeze
steps.body: $\lim_{x\to0}\cos x = 1$ and the upper bound is 1, so $\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sin x}{x} = 1$.

pitfalls: Using L'Hôpital's rule — it needs the derivative of $\sin x$, which is itself proved from this limit (circular).

cse-1995-b-56.approach: Compute FIRST and FOLLOW, then put each production $X\to\alpha$ under FIRST($\alpha$), and under FOLLOW($X$) when $\alpha$ can be λ.

steps.title: FIRST sets
steps.body:
- FIRST(Var) = {id} (rule 6)
- FIRST(Expr) = {\_, (, id} (rules 1, 2, 3 via Var)
- FIRST(ExprTail) = {\_, λ} (rules 4, 5)
- FIRST(VarTail) = {(, λ} (rules 7, 8)
- FIRST(Goal) = FIRST(Expr) = {\_, (, id}

steps.title: FOLLOW sets
steps.body:
- Rule 9: \$ ∈ FOLLOW(Expr). Rules 2 and 7: ) ∈ FOLLOW(Expr).
- Rules 1 and 4: Expr ends Expr and ExprTail, and rule 3: ExprTail ends Expr, so FOLLOW(Expr) = FOLLOW(ExprTail) = {\$, )}.
- Rule 3: FOLLOW(Var) = (FIRST(ExprTail) − λ) ∪ FOLLOW(Expr) = {\_, \$, )}.
- Rule 6: FOLLOW(VarTail) = FOLLOW(Var) = {\_, \$, )}.

steps.title: Fill rows from FIRST
steps.body: Expr: \_ → 1, ( → 2, id → 3. ExprTail: \_ → 4. Var: id → 6. VarTail: ( → 7. Goal: \_, (, id → 9.

steps.title: λ-rules from FOLLOW
steps.body:
Rule 5 (ExprTail → λ) goes under FOLLOW(ExprTail) = {), \$}. Rule 8 (VarTail → λ) goes under FOLLOW(VarTail) = {\_, ), \$}.

No cell holds two rules, so the grammar is LL(1).

pitfalls: Forgetting that _ ∈ FOLLOW(VarTail) (via FIRST(ExprTail)), which puts rule 8 under _.
Leaving ) out of FOLLOW(Expr) — it comes from rules 2 and 7.
cse-1995-b-56.verification: Parsed the input id ( id ) \$ with the table: Goal→9, Expr→3, Var→6, match id, VarTail→7, … every lookup hit exactly one rule and the input was accepted.

cse-1995-b-57-a.approach: Unary minus binds tighter than *, and the parentheses group b+c first, so the tree is * over a and uminus(+(b, c)).

steps.title: Parse structure
steps.body: $a * -(b+c)$ = $a * (\text{uminus}(b+c))$: the operand of * on the right is the negated parenthesised sum.

steps.title: Tree
steps.body: Root `*`; left child `a`; right child `uminus`, whose single child is `+` with children `b` and `c`.

answer.value: Root *, left child a, right child unary minus whose child is + with children b and c

pitfalls: Treating the minus as binary subtraction — there is no left operand, so it is a unary operator node with one child.
cse-1995-b-57-a.verification: Postorder of the tree is `a b c + uminus *`, which evaluates to $a\cdot(-(b+c))$.

cse-1995-b-57-b.approach: Show that a cycle makes the grammar ambiguous: one parse tree for a string can be extended by inserting the cycle, giving a second tree. Ambiguous grammars are never LL(1).

steps.title: Set-up
steps.body: Let $A \Rightarrow^+ A$, with A a useful nonterminal (reachable from the start symbol and deriving some terminal string $w$, so $A\Rightarrow^* w$). Take a parse tree $T$ of $w$ rooted at A.

steps.title: Two parse trees
steps.body: The derivation $A\Rightarrow^+ A$ gives a partial tree $C$ whose root is A and whose only nonterminal leaf is A; its other leaves derive λ. Plugging $T$ into that leaf gives a tree $T'$ for the same $w$ (the λ leaves add nothing). $T'$ has more nodes than $T$, so the two trees are different. Embedding both under a derivation from the start symbol gives two parse trees for one sentence: the grammar is **ambiguous**.

steps.title: Not LL(1)
steps.body:
An LL(1) table gives at most one production per (nonterminal, lookahead) pair, so a predictive parser builds at most one leftmost derivation per sentence. LL(1) grammars are therefore unambiguous. A grammar with a cycle is ambiguous, so it **cannot be LL(1)**.

Directly: when A is on the stack with lookahead $a$ = first symbol of $w$, both the production that starts the cycle and the one that starts $T$ predict $a$ (or they coincide, and the parser loops for ever), so the table cell $M[A,a]$ has a conflict.

answer.value: If $A \Rightarrow^+ A$ and $A \Rightarrow^* w$, then $w$ has two parse trees from A (with and without the cycle inserted), so the grammar is ambiguous; every LL(1) grammar is unambiguous, so a grammar with cycles cannot be LL(1).

pitfalls: Arguing only from left recursion — a cycle such as $A\to B$, $B\to A$ is not immediately left recursive, but the ambiguity argument still applies.
cse-1995-b-57-b.verification: Example: $S\to S \mid a$. The string $a$ has trees $S\to a$ and $S\to S\to a$, and $M[S,a]$ holds both productions.

cse-1995-b-58-a.approach: In Pascal, `with R do` opens the field names of record R as the innermost scope, so they hide the outer variables of the same name inside the with-body. The name after `with` itself is resolved in the enclosing scope.

steps.title: Declarations available
steps.body: Inside T: parameters U, V, X, Y; local variable **A** (record with fields A, B) and local variable **B** (record with fields B, A).

steps.title: First with-statement
steps.body:
`with A do`: the `A` after `with` is the local record variable A. Inside the body, the fields of A hide the outer names:

- `A := 4` → field **A.A**
- `B := V` → field **A.B** (V is the parameter)

steps.title: Second with-statement
steps.body:
`with B do`: the `B` after `with` is the local record variable B (the with-scope of A has closed). Inside:

- `A := X` → field **B.A**
- `B := Y` → field **B.B**

(X and Y are the parameters.)

answer.value: In `with A do`, A and B denote the fields A.A and A.B of record variable A; in `with B do`, A and B denote the fields B.A and B.B of record variable B; the names after `with` refer to the local record variables.

pitfalls: Reading `B := V` inside `with A do` as the record variable B — the field A.B hides it.
cse-1995-b-58-a.verification: Type check: every assignment puts an integer into an integer field, which is only valid with this resolution (assigning an integer to a whole record variable would be a type error).

cse-1995-b-58-b.approach: A lexical error is a character sequence that cannot form any token. Split the statement into lexemes and check each one; misplaced but valid tokens are syntax errors, not lexical errors.

steps.title: Tokenise
steps.body:
`if` `A` `>` `1` `,` `then` `B` `=` `2.5` `A` `else` `read` `(` `C` `)` `;`

Each is a valid Pascal token (keyword, identifier, relational operator, integer, comma, real number, parentheses, semicolon).

steps.title: Classify the mistakes
steps.body:
- `,` before `then` — valid token in the wrong place → **syntax** error.
- `=` instead of `:=` — `=` is a valid relational token → **syntax** error.
- `2.5A` — a scanner reads the longest real `2.5`, then the identifier `A`; the token pair is the problem → **syntax** error. (A strict reading of the Pascal standard, which requires a separator between a number and an identifier, would call this the one lexical error.)

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: No lexeme is malformed, so there are **no lexical errors**; all the mistakes are caught by the parser.

answer.value: No lexical error: every lexeme (if, A, >, 1, ',', then, B, =, 2.5, A, else, read, (, C, ), ;) is a valid Pascal token; the mistakes (',' before then, '=' instead of ':=', 2.5A) are syntax errors.

pitfalls: Calling every visible mistake a lexical error — the scanner only rejects character sequences that form no token.
cse-1995-b-58-b.verification: Matched each lexeme against the Pascal token classes (keywords, identifiers, unsigned numbers, special symbols); all match.

cse-1995-b-59.approach: Build a nondeterministic poly-time machine for $L^C$: on input x of length n, guess the unique string y of length n in L together with an NP certificate that $y\in L$, verify it, and accept iff $y\ne x$.

steps.title: Key observation
steps.body:
Exactly one string $y_n$ of length n lies in L. So for $|x| = n$:

$$x \in L^C \iff x \ne y_n \iff \exists y\,\big(|y| = n \wedge y\in L \wedge y \ne x\big).$$

steps.title: Verifier for L^C
steps.body:
Since $L\in NP$ it has a poly-time verifier $V(y,c)$ with certificates of length $\le p(|y|)$. A certificate for $x\in L^C$ is a pair $(y, c)$ with $|y| = |x|$. Check:

1. $|y| = |x|$ and $y \ne x$ — $O(n)$;
2. $V(y, c)$ accepts — polynomial in $n$.

The certificate length is $n + p(n)$, a polynomial.

steps.title: Correctness
steps.body:
- If $x\notin L$: take $y = y_n$ (it is in L and $\ne x$) with its certificate; the check accepts.
- If $x\in L$: then $x = y_n$ is the only length-n string in L, so any $y$ with $|y|=n$ and $y\in L$ equals x; check 1 fails. No certificate is accepted.

Hence $L^C$ has a poly-time verifier, so $L^C\in NP$.

answer.value: Certificate for $x \in L^C$ ($|x| = n$): a string $y$ with $|y| = n$, $y \ne x$, plus an NP certificate that $y \in L$. Since L has exactly one string of each length, such a $y$ exists iff $x \notin L$, and checking it takes polynomial time, so $L^C \in$ NP.

pitfalls: Trying to negate the NP verifier for L directly — NP is not known to be closed under complement; the "exactly one string per length" condition is what makes this work.
cse-1995-b-59.verification: Example: $L=\{0^n\}$ (in P ⊆ NP). For $x = 0010$ the certificate $y = 0000$ works; for $x = 0000$ no $y \ne x$ of length 4 is in L.

cse-1995-b-60.approach: Each bubble-sort pass compares adjacent pairs left to right and swaps out-of-order ones, so the largest remaining element moves to the end. Trace the five passes.
pitfalls: Doing only one swap per pass — a pass carries the larger element all the way along.
cse-1995-b-60.verification: After pass k the last k elements are the k largest in order: pass 3 ends with 37, 52, 92. ✓

cse-1995-b-61.approach: Build the truth table; the principal CNF is the AND of one maxterm per row where the formula is false (a variable appears plain if it is 0 in that row, negated if it is 1).

steps.title: Where the formula is true
steps.body: $(p\wedge q)$ is true for $pqr = 110, 111$; $(\neg q\wedge r)$ is true for $pqr = 001, 101$. So $f=1$ on rows 001, 101, 110, 111 and $f = 0$ on **000, 010, 011, 100**.

steps.title: Maxterms for the false rows
steps.body:
| $pqr$ | maxterm |
|---|---|
| 000 | $p\vee q\vee r$ |
| 010 | $p\vee\neg q\vee r$ |
| 011 | $p\vee\neg q\vee\neg r$ |
| 100 | $\neg p\vee q\vee r$ |

steps.title: Principal CNF
steps.body:
$$(p\vee q\vee r)\wedge(p\vee
eg q\vee r)\wedge(p\vee
eg q\vee
eg r)\wedge(
eg p\vee q\vee r)$$
i.e. $\prod M(0,2,3,4)$.

answer.value:
$(p\vee q\vee r)\wedge(p\vee
eg q\vee r)\wedge(p\vee
eg q\vee
eg r)\wedge(
eg p\vee q\vee r)$

pitfalls: Writing the literal un-negated when the variable is 1 in the false row — maxterms use the opposite polarity to minterms.
cse-1995-b-61.verification: The minterms are {1, 5, 6, 7} and the maxterms {0, 2, 3, 4}; together they cover all 8 rows with no overlap.

cse-1995-b-62-a.approach: Tracks per surface = radial band width / track pitch. Unformatted capacity = surfaces × tracks × sectors × 4000 bytes; formatting takes 96 bytes of each sector.

steps.title: Tracks per surface
steps.body: Radial band $= (12 - 4)/2 = 4\text{ cm} = 40\text{ mm}$. Tracks $= 40 / 0.1 = 400$.

pitfalls: Using the full diameter difference (8 cm) as the band width — the tracks span the radius difference (4 cm) on each surface.

cse-1995-b-62-b.approach: In one revolution the head passes one whole track. Effective (data) rate = formatted data bytes per track × revolutions per second.

steps.title: Revolutions per second
steps.body: $3600\text{ rpm} / 60 = 60$ revolutions per second.

steps.title: Data per track
steps.body: $20 \text{ sectors} \times (4000-96) = 20\times3904 = 78{,}080$ bytes.

steps.title: Effective rate
steps.body: $78{,}080 \times 60 = 4{,}684{,}800$ bytes/s (≈ 4.68 MB/s). The raw rate, counting overhead, would be $20\times4000\times60 = 4{,}800{,}000$ bytes/s.

pitfalls: Counting the 96 overhead bytes as transferred data — only the 3904 data bytes reach memory.

cse-1995-b-63-a.approach: Use De Morgan: $\overline{A}+\overline{B}+C = \overline{A\cdot B\cdot\overline{C}}$, which is a 3-input NAND of A, B and $\overline{C}$; the inverter supplies $\overline{C}$.

steps.title: Rewrite
steps.body: $C = \overline{\overline{C}}$, so $Z = \overline{A}+\overline{B}+\overline{\overline{C}} = \overline{A\cdot B\cdot \overline{C}}$ (De Morgan).

steps.title: Circuit
steps.body: Feed C through the inverter; feed A, B and $\overline{C}$ into a 3-input NAND gate. Its output is Z. With $A=1, B=1, C=0$ the NAND inputs are all 1, so $Z=0$ — the only input that makes $\overline{A}+\overline{B}+C$ false.

answer.value: Invert C, then Z = NAND(A, B, $\overline{C}$)

pitfalls: Inverting A and B instead — that needs three inverters and an OR, not one inverter and a NAND.
cse-1995-b-63-a.verification: Truth check: Z = 0 only for $A=B=1, C=0$ in both $\overline{A}+\overline{B}+C$ and NAND(A, B, $\overline{C}$).
